An Australian Government agency, or an organisation (generally a business with annual turnover above $3 million, or one of the smaller businesses the Act names), that must comply with the APPs.
Unauthorised access to, disclosure of or loss of personal information that is likely to result in serious harm to an individual, where remedial action has not removed that likelihood.
The Australian Information Commissioner, who receives data breach statements and regulates compliance with the Act.
Information about racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, criminal record and similar matters, and health, genetic and biometric information.

Collection, use, retention and sharing of personal information is limited to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the purposes it was collected for.
A business implements reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the personal information.

glossary.definition: The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, California's law giving consumers rights over the personal information businesses collect about them.

A person that processes personal information on behalf of a business under a written contract that restricts its use of that information.
To sell is to disclose personal information to a third party for money or other valuable consideration; to share is to disclose it for cross-context behavioral advertising.
Personal information such as government identifiers, account credentials, precise geolocation, racial or ethnic origin, health data and the contents of private communications.
A request from a consumer, or someone authorized to act for them, that the business can reasonably verify comes from the consumer the information is about.

cis-controls.scoring: Percentage of applicable controls implemented, with partial implementation counting as half. CIS defines no certification score; this percentage is an HCG readiness measure.
cis-controls.notice: HCG readiness control set organized by the 18 CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1. The names of the 18 Controls are taken from CIS's public list; the Safeguards, their numbering and the Implementation Group assignments are published by CIS under a non-commercial licence and are not reproduced. Controls here are HCG-written, carry HCG numbering, and note the lowest Implementation Group they correspond to.
applies: Controls apply according to the organization's target Implementation Group: an IG1 organization is assessed on controls marked IG1; IG2 adds those marked IG2; IG3 adds those marked IG3. Controls above the target group are marked not applicable.

glossary.definition: A prioritized set of 18 cybersecurity controls published by the Center for Internet Security.
A specific action within a CIS Control. Version 8.1 has 153 Safeguards.

CIS's tiers for prioritizing Safeguards: IG1 is essential cyber hygiene for every organization, IG2 adds Safeguards for organizations with more complex IT, and IG3 adds Safeguards for organizations facing sophisticated attacks.

families.name: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
Inventory and Control of Software Assets
Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

cisa-ztmm.name: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model
cisa-ztmm.full_name: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model, Version 2.0 (April 2023)
cisa-ztmm.scoring: A function is rated by the highest stage it fully reaches: Traditional (no stage met), Initial, Advanced or Optimal (all three stages met). The percentage counts Optimal functions in full and Initial or Advanced as half; it is an HCG summary, and CISA's own measure is the stage per function.
cisa-ztmm.notice: Each function of the five pillars and the cross-cutting capabilities is assessed against CISA's maturity stages. The Traditional stage is the function's starting point; the Initial, Advanced and Optimal stage descriptions are the test points. All text is CISA's.
applies: Stages build on each other: each subsequent stage requires greater protection, detail and complexity, so a stage is met only if the stages below it are met. Agencies may sit at different stages for different functions.

glossary.definition: An approach where access to resources is limited to only those who need it and only for the resources needed, with decisions made per request based on continuously evaluated trust.
CISA's five zero trust areas: Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, and Data.
Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and Governance, which support all five pillars.
Traditional, Initial, Advanced and Optimal: the progression from manual, static configuration to automated, dynamic, fully integrated zero trust.

applies: Level 1 uses the SP 800-171A objectives of the mapped requirement; wherever an objective says CUI, read it as FCI.

Supplier Performance Risk System, where contractors record assessment results and affirmations.

cmmc-l2.name: CMMC Level 2

Controlled Unclassified Information: government information that is not classified but must still be protected.

Supplier Performance Risk System, where contractors record assessment scores and affirmations.

Federal Information Processing Standards; FIPS 140 validation confirms a cryptographic module has been independently tested.

cmmc-l3.name: CMMC Level 3

applies: Where an assessment objective uses an organization-defined or periodic interval, the interval may be no longer than one year.

glossary.definition: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification, the Department of Defense program that verifies contractors protect federal contract and controlled information.

Defense Contract Management Agency.

System Security Plan: the document that describes the system in scope and how each requirement is implemented.
Supplier Performance Risk System, where contractors record assessment results and affirmations.
Advanced persistent threat: a well-resourced adversary that pursues long-term access to a target.

coppa.name: COPPA Rule
coppa.full_name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (16 CFR Part 312), implementing the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
coppa.scoring: Percentage of applicable requirements that are implemented. The Rule defines no score; this percentage is an HCG measure of progress.
applies: Verifiable parental consent is obtained before any collection, use or disclosure of personal information from children.
A child's participation in an activity may not be conditioned on disclosing more personal information than is reasonably necessary to take part.
The operator maintains a written information security program with safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the children's information and to the operator's size, complexity and activities.

glossary.definition: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, implemented by the FTC's Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule.
An individual under the age of 13.
A person who operates a commercial website or online service directed to children, or who knowingly collects personal information from children online.

A reasonable effort, taking available technology into account, to ensure that a child's parent is told about the operator's information practices and authorizes them before the child's personal information is collected.
Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. agency that issues and enforces the COPPA Rule.

Prohibition against conditioning a child's participation on collection of personal information

cyber-essentials.notice: Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0 (Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3, UK Crown Copyright, April 2026). applies: Authentication to cloud services always uses multi-factor authentication.

glossary.definition: The UK government-backed scheme, run by the NCSC, certifying that an organisation has five basic technical controls in place to protect against common internet-based attacks.
The National Cyber Security Centre, the UK's technical authority for cyber security.
Multi-factor authentication: proving identity with more than one kind of factor, such as a password and a code from a trusted device.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System; Cyber Essentials treats a CVSS v3 base score of 7 or above as critical or high risk.

dora.name: DORA
dora.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 of the European Parliament and of the Council on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (Digital Operational Resilience Act)
dora.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
dora.scoring: Percentage of applicable obligations that are implemented. The Regulation defines no score; this percentage is an HCG measure of progress.
dora.notice: Assessed against the text of the Regulation. The regulatory and implementing technical standards adopted under it specify many of these obligations in more detail and are not part of this assessment.
applies: Chapter II is implemented in proportion to the entity's size, overall risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of its services, activities and operations.
Paragraphs that apply to financial entities "other than microenterprises" are not applicable to a microenterprise.

The small entities listed in Article 16(1) follow the simplified ICT risk management framework of that article instead of Articles 5 to 15; for them the obligations in those articles are not applicable.
The management body defines, approves, oversees and is responsible for the ICT risk management framework.
A register of information on all contractual arrangements for ICT services is maintained at entity, sub-consolidated and consolidated levels.
A major ICT-related incident is reported in three stages: an initial notification, an intermediate report and a final report, within time limits set by technical standards.

glossary.definition: The Digital Operational Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, which sets ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party risk requirements for financial entities in the European Union.
Information and communication technology.
An undertaking that provides ICT services to a financial entity.
A function whose disruption would materially impair the financial entity's financial performance, the soundness or continuity of its services, or its continued compliance with its authorisation.
Threat-led penetration testing: a controlled attempt to compromise the entity's live production systems that mimics the tactics of real threat actors.
The European Supervisory Authorities: the European Banking Authority, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority and the European Securities and Markets Authority.

families.name: Backup policies and procedures, restoration and recovery procedures and methods

Reporting of major ICT-related incidents and voluntary notification of significant cyber threats

Testing of ICT tools and systems

easa-part-is-d.name: EASA Part-IS.D.OR
easa-part-is-d.full_name: EASA Part-IS.D.OR: Information security organisation requirements (Annex to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1645) for Part-21 design and production organisations, aerodrome operators and apron management service providers, and, from 27 March 2031, certain ground handling organisations
easa-part-is-d.issuing_body: European Commission; European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)
easa-part-is-d.scoring: Part-IS has no official score. The compliance percentage is the share of applicable requirements assessed compliant; any non-compliance is a finding that needs a corrective action plan.
applies: Applies to the organisations listed in Article 2(1): Part-21 design and production organisations (except those solely involved with ELA2 aircraft), and aerodrome operators and apron management service providers under Part-ADR.OR.

The competent authority may approve an organisation not implementing IS.D.OR.200(a) to (d) and IS.D.OR.205 to IS.D.OR.260, based on a documented risk assessment showing no information security risk with a potential impact on aviation safety. Reporting under Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 and IS.D.OR.200(a)(13) still apply.

glossary.definition: European Union Aviation Safety Agency, which issues the acceptable means of compliance and guidance material for Part-IS.
The EU aviation information security rules: organisation requirements in Regulation (EU) 2023/203 (Part-IS.D.OR) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1645 (Part-IS.D.OR).
Information security management system: the processes, procedures, roles and responsibilities an organisation uses to manage information security risks with a potential impact on aviation safety.
Information security management manual: the document that describes the organisation's ISMS and is made available to the competent authority.
Acceptable means of compliance: EASA's non-binding standards by which an organisation can show it meets a requirement.
Guidance material: EASA's non-binding material that explains a requirement or its AMC.
Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 748/2012: certification of aircraft and related products, and approval of design and production organisations.
European Light Aircraft 2: a defined class of light aeroplanes, sailplanes, balloons and airships (Regulation (EU) No 748/2012, Article 1(2)(j)).
Apron management services, regulated with aerodromes under Part-ADR.OR.

easa-part-is-i.name: EASA Part-IS.I.OR
easa-part-is-i.full_name: EASA Part-IS.I.OR: Information security organisation requirements (Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/203) for Part-145 maintenance organisations, CAMOs, air operators, ATOs, aircrew aero-medical centres, FSTD operators, ATCO training organisations and aero-medical centres, ATM/ANS providers, U-space and single common information service providers, and ATM/ANS design and production organisations
easa-part-is-i.issuing_body: European Commission; European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)

applies: Applies to the organisations listed in Article 2(1): Part-145 maintenance organisations and CAMOs (except Part-ML only), air operators (with small-aircraft exceptions), ATOs, aircrew aero-medical centres, FSTD operators, ATCO training organisations and aero-medical centres, ATM/ANS providers (with exceptions), U-space and single common information service providers, and approved ATM/ANS design or production organisations.

Reporting under Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 and IS.I.OR.200(a)(13) still apply.

glossary.definition: European Union Aviation Safety Agency, which issues the acceptable means of compliance and guidance material for Part-IS.

Continuing airworthiness management organisation approved under Part-CAMO.
Approved training organisation under Part-ORA.
Flight simulation training device.
Air traffic management and air navigation services.

essential-eight.name: Essential Eight
essential-eight.issuing_body: Australian Signals Directorate, Australian Cyber Security Centre
essential-eight.scoring: Percentage of applicable strategy levels implemented, with partial counting as half. ASD measures maturity per strategy: a strategy is at a maturity level only when every requirement of that level is met. This percentage is an HCG readiness measure.
essential-eight.notice: Requirements are quoted from the ASD Essential Eight Maturity Model, published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (© Commonwealth of Australia). Each mitigation strategy has a control per maturity level; assess the controls for the target maturity level and mark the others not applicable.
applies: Organisations choose a target maturity level based on the tradecraft and targeting they aim to mitigate; only the controls for that level apply and the others are marked not applicable.
Each maturity level's requirements are listed in full in its own appendix, so a level is assessed on its own list.

glossary.definition: ASD's eight prioritised mitigation strategies: patch applications, patch operating systems, multi-factor authentication, restrict administrative privileges, application control, restrict Microsoft Office macros, user application hardening and regular backups.
Maturity Level One to Three, each aimed at mitigating a higher level of adversary tradecraft and targeting; Maturity Level Zero means weaknesses remain.

eu-ai-act.name: EU AI Act

eu-ai-act.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
eu-ai-act.scoring: Percentage of applicable obligations that are implemented. The Regulation defines no score; this percentage is an HCG measure of progress.
eu-ai-act.notice: Assessed against the text of the Regulation as published in the Official Journal on 12 July 2024. Application dates are those of Article 113 as published; a later amending act may have changed them.
applies: The high-risk obligations apply to AI systems that are safety components of products under the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and require third-party conformity assessment, and to the systems listed in Annex III.

Providers of general-purpose AI models released under a free and open-source licence with public parameters are exempt from the documentation duties of Article 53(1)(a) and (b), unless the model has systemic risk.

glossary.definition: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the European Union's law setting rules for AI systems and general-purpose AI models according to the risk they pose.
The organisation that develops an AI system or general-purpose AI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name.
The organisation that uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity.

An AI system that is a safety component of a regulated product, or that is used in one of the areas listed in Annex III, such as employment, education, essential services, law enforcement and critical infrastructure.
An AI model that can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks and can be integrated into many downstream systems.
The European Commission's function for supervising general-purpose AI models and supporting implementation of the Regulation.

Vulnerabilities are handled for a support period of at least five years, or the expected time in use if that is shorter.

glossary.definition: The Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the European Union's law setting cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements.
A software or hardware product and its remote data processing solutions, including components placed on the market separately.
The organisation that develops or manufactures a product with digital elements, or has it designed, developed or manufactured, and markets it under its own name or trademark.
The period during which a manufacturer must ensure that vulnerabilities of a product with digital elements are handled effectively.

Computer security incident response team; the CSIRT designated as coordinator receives vulnerability and incident notifications.

Acquisition of unencrypted customer information without the authorization of the individual to whom it pertains (16 CFR 314.2).
Multi-factor authentication: verification of at least two of knowledge, possession and inherence factors.

gdpr.name: GDPR
gdpr.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation)
gdpr.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
gdpr.scoring: Percentage of applicable obligations that are implemented. The Regulation defines no score; this percentage is an HCG measure of progress.
gdpr.notice: Assessed against the text of the Regulation. Member State law adopted under it, and guidelines of the European Data Protection Board, may add to or specify these obligations.
applies: The controller is responsible for compliance with the processing principles and must be able to demonstrate it.

Records of processing are not required of an organisation with fewer than 250 employees, unless its processing is likely to result in a risk to individuals, is not occasional, or includes special category or criminal offence data.
A data protection impact assessment is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals.

A data protection officer is mandatory for public authorities and for organisations whose core activities are large-scale regular and systematic monitoring or large-scale processing of special category or criminal offence data.

glossary.definition: The General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the European Union's law on the processing of personal data.
The organisation that decides why and how personal data are processed.
An organisation that processes personal data on behalf of a controller.
The identified or identifiable person the personal data relate to.

Feedback about efficacy of measurement is gathered and assessed.

nydfs-500.name: NYDFS 23 NYCRR 500

nydfs-500.scoring: Percentage of applicable sections 500.2 to 500.17 that are compliant. Class A subsections apply only to Class A companies, and sections lifted by an exemption in 500.19 are not applicable. The regulation defines no score; DFS asks only whether the entity materially complied (500.17(b)). This percentage is an HCG measure of progress.
applies: Class A requirements apply to a covered entity with at least $20 million gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years (from the entity and its New York affiliates) and either over 2,000 employees or over $1 billion group gross annual revenue.

An entity with fewer than 20 employees and contractors, or under $7.5 million gross annual revenue in each of the last three fiscal years, or under $15 million year-end total assets, is exempt from the listed sections. MFA is still required for remote access, remote access to third-party applications with nonpublic information, and privileged accounts (500.12(a)).
An employee, agent, wholly owned subsidiary or similar that is itself a covered entity is exempt to the extent it is covered by another covered entity's cybersecurity program.

An entity that neither operates or controls information systems nor holds or is required to hold nonpublic information is exempt from most technical sections; 500.9, 500.11, 500.13 and 500.17 still apply.
An Insurance Law article 70 (captive) entity holding no nonpublic information other than its parent's or affiliates' has the same exemption as 500.19(c).

Multi-factor authentication: verification of at least two of knowledge, possession and inherence factors (500.1(j)).
Business continuity and disaster recovery.
